nutshell: Vehicle ReID is mostly studied under daytime/favorable lighting, and unlike person ReID, nighttime vehicle matching can't just be reframed as a visible-infrared modality-gap problem because near-infrared cameras are impractical for traffic scenes (cost, resolution, glare from headlights/streetlights). This paper defines Day-Night cross-domain vehicle ReID (DN-ReID) - same visible spectrum, day vs. night domain gap - contributes two new benchmark datasets, and proposes DNDM, a ResNet-50-based framework combining glare suppression, gradient-based structural feature enhancement, and cross-domain class-activation-map exchange.
contributions: First formalization of DN-ReID as distinct from visible-infrared ReID (same modality, day/night domain gap rather than sensor-modality gap), with two new datasets: DN-Wild (2,286 IDs, 140,897 images, repurposed from the testing set of VERI-Wild 2.0, heavily day/night-imbalanced) and DN-348 (348 IDs, ~50 day + 50 night images per vehicle, self-collected across a 400km2 city-scale camera network over 4 months, deliberately sample-balanced).

Night-domain Glare Suppression (NGS): thresholds a grayscale nighttime image (brightness > 220) into a binary glare mask, then learns a single linear projection over the concatenated feature+mask to produce a suppression mask that's subtracted from the raw feature (Eq. 3-6) - a lightweight, mostly-heuristic mechanism rather than a learned segmentation network.

Dual-domain Structure Enhancement (DSE): computes non-negative pixel-wise local gradients within an NxN window and aggregates them into a structural descriptor added back to the appearance feature (Eq. 7-9), motivated by the idea that geometric/structural cues survive illumination change better than raw appearance.

Cross-domain Class Awareness (CCA): during training only, multiplies each domain's projected features by the other domain's class activation map (Eq. 12) at every ResNet-50 stage, explicitly pushing day and night branches toward class-consistent activations.
deficiencies: The paper's own text describes a DN-Wild Night-to-Day mAP gain over the BOT baseline of 0.2 percentage points (0.398 -> 0.400) as DNDM 'significantly improves' performance - on the paper's own hardest, most realistic dataset (DN-Wild has severe day/night sample imbalance, unlike the curated DN-348), the actual margin is essentially noise-level.

Table 2 shows the plain BOT baseline (no day-night-specific design at all) is the best or second-best method on 3 of 4 DN-Wild metrics (Day-to-Night Rank-5 and mAP, Night-to-Day mAP), beating most of the purpose-adapted VI-ReID methods (DDAG, LbA, AGW, CAJ, DCL, PMT) - undercutting the framing that this task specifically requires specialized day-night modules, at least on the larger/harder of the two datasets.

The NGS glare-detection step relies on one fixed, hand-picked brightness threshold (220) rather than a learned or adaptive mechanism, despite DN-348 spanning many different cameras, locations, and 4 months of varying real-world lighting conditions across a 400km2 network - no sensitivity analysis is given for how robust this single threshold is across that diversity.

All results are single-run numbers on only two datasets, with no variance/seed reporting and no computational-cost comparison (added latency/parameters from stacking three new modules across all four ResNet stages) against the plain ResNet-50 baseline, despite the paper's own motivation citing real-time traffic surveillance as the target application.
notable: The CCA module's cross-domain feature exchange is explicitly training-only - the paper states the class activation maps are 'not exchanged during the test phase' - so the deployed inference-time model never actually fuses day/night information directly; CCA functions purely as a training-time regularizer, not a test-time cross-domain fusion mechanism, which is easy to miss from the framework name and diagram alone. Also worth flagging: DN-Wild is built from the *testing* split of an existing public dataset (VERI-Wild 2.0) rather than independently collected data, so any future model that was pretrained on or exposed to VERI-Wild 2.0's test set risks evaluation leakage when benchmarked on DN-Wild.
